quote: With one request, reading the target weights dominates the per-step latency (Figure 2 a), so verifying additional tokens adds little extra latency. Stock still verifies only one drafted chain, ignoring the other candidates that its drafter ranks at each position, which often include the target’s next token. Using them would accept about twice as many tokens per step (§ 3.1 ). With batching, each request adds its own attention, recurrent-state and prefill work, so weight reads no longer dominate the step, and stock’s speedup over AR decoding roughly halves (Figure 2 b). Existing techniques such as draft trees [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] and batch-aware speculation [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] are general, but the best choice depends on the deployment. A deployment comprises a serving regime, a drafter, a target and a GPU platform, and each changes what pays off. The serving regime can turn a gain into a loss. Checking drafts with a low-precision target copy before the exact pass speeds up decoding with one request, but with batching on BF16 Qwen3.8-27B the same idea is 13% slower, because the extra check takes nearly a step. The drafter decides how to score a draft tree. DSpark conditions each drafted token on the one before it, and a tree that ignores this accepts half the tokens of one using it. The target and the GPU decide what each mechanism costs. A tree on hybrid Qwen3.8-27B [ 14 ] must track every node’s recurrent state (§ 2.3 ), and the RTX PRO 6000 lacks Hopper’s wgmma instructions, so kernels need porting. No universal optimization fits every deployment. Figure 2: (a) Single-request step time split into target weights and the rest, at peak bandwidth and as measured after the first optimization round. Reading the weights dominates the step. (b) Stock speedup over AR falls as the batch size grows, for Qwen3.8-27B in FP8 and Qwen3.5-4B in BF16. (c) Task accuracy change against stock, with 95% CIs, for a lossless system and a faulty one with an injected logit bias. All four intervals include zero, so accuracy cannot flag the faulty systems. Manually optimizing each deployment does not scale, whereas coding agents [ 15 , 16 ] iterate rapidly. This makes per-deployment optimization a natural fit for them, and agentic optimizers such as AlphaEvolve and ADRS already evolve programs against automated evaluators [ 17 , 18 ] . For lossless speculative decoding, however, building a reliable evaluator is difficult for two reasons. First, many gains are only a few percent, close to timing noise, and a gain measured on development requests may not generalize to unseen ones. Second, an agent rewarded for speed is prone to reward hacking [ 19 , 20 ] , such as adopting a faster numerical shortcut that changes outputs without a measurable drop in task accuracy (Figure 2 c). We present SpecPilot (Figure 3 ), an autonomous agentic loop that searches for speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment. It rests on four ideas. First, a cost model compares measured performance with an estimated ceiling to locate where speed is lost. Second, parallel agents explore multiple directions on separate GPUs and integrate the validated pieces, so small gains add up. Third, a controller isolated from the agents accepts a change only on a significant gain confirmed on unseen requests, and token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect lossy changes (§ 3.3 ). Finally, validated optimizations are distilled into a structured memory as replayable code and evidence, for reuse in later rounds and new deployments. Figure 3: One round of the SpecPilot loop. 0 The cost model measures the gap between the current system and its ceiling. 1 Directions run in parallel, one per GPU. 2 Validated pieces stack into one system. 3 A kernel sub-agent tunes the kernels furthest from their byte floors. 4 Token forcing checks the sealed final against stock at every teacher-forced token. Each round distills its mechanisms into memory entries, which carry to later rounds and new deployments. The loop developed lossless techniques, each targeting a gap the cost model measured (§ 4 ). Best-first tree verification exploits idle drafter candidates, even on hybrid recurrent targets, and W12, a general lossless 12-bit weight format, cuts the weight reads dominating single-request steps. Two-level verification pre-checks drafts at low precision, nearly doubling accepted tokens per exact pass. For batching, three mechanisms spend verify rows where they pay off (§ 4.4 ). We evaluate SpecPilot on four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock’s 4.46 × \times to 10.87 × \times with one request (Figure 1 ), and from 1.94 × \times to 3.93 × \times with batching. On H100 with one request, it is 1.84 × \times faster than DDTree [ 10 ] . In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: [topsep=2pt,partopsep=0pt,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt] • Autonomous Optimization Loop: We design SpecPilot, a ceiling-guided agentic framework that tailors speculative decoding to each deployment and transfers validated optimizations across hardware and models via a structured memory. To prevent reward hacking, we introduce token forcing, a stock-calibrated test that detects output divergences task accuracy misses. • Discovered Lossless Algorithms: SpecPilot discovered W12, a general lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three mechanisms for batching. • Cross-Regime Bottleneck Analysis: We show how ceiling-guided discovery adapts to both memory-bandwidth and per-row compute bottlenecks, and why the same mechanism can accelerate one request but slow decoding with batching on the same GPU. ## 2 Background ## 2.1 Speculative Decoding In speculative decoding [ 1 , 2 ] , a drafter proposes m m tokens x ^ 1 . . m \hat{x}_{1..m} after the prefix x < t x_{<t} , and the target model verifies them in one forward pass, one row per token. Greedy decoding accepts the longest prefix with x ^ i = arg max p ( ⋅ ∣ x < t , x ^ < i ) \hat{x}_{i}=\arg\max p(\cdot\mid x_{<t},\hat{x}_{<i}) and adds the target’s argmax as a bonus, accepting τ ∈ [ 1 , m + 1 ] \tau\in[1,m+1] tokens. Lossless. A system is lossless if every accepted token lies on a path verified by a pass over the exact target weights ( exact pass ) and equals that pass’s argmax. Its output is then the target’s greedy decode up to floating-point reduction order, such as GEMM tiling or tree attention, which can change a token only at a logit near-tie. Stock already differs from AR in this way. At each first divergence, the two tokens’ log-probabilities differ by at most 0.232 nats (§ 3.3 ). A low-precision verify pass, by contrast, can change tokens even far from near-ties. This makes losslessness hard to test. Requiring identical outputs rejects lossless systems, and task accuracy misses faulty ones (Figure 2 c). Token forcing (§ 3.3 ) instead checks every token statistically against stock. ## 2.2 Parallel Drafters and Draft Trees DFlash2 [ 5 ] , like DFlash [ 4 ] , drafts a block of masked positions in one pass from target hidden states. A low-rank selector scores each of the top-16 candidates per position given one at the previous position, and candidates and scores form the lattice . DSpark [ 6 ] adds a Markov head on the previous token: | ℓ s ​ ( y ) = base s ​ ( y ) + ⟨ W 1 ​ [ x s − 1 ] , W 2 ​ [ y ] ⟩ , \ell_{s}(y)=\mathrm{base}_{s}(y)+\big\langle W_{1}[x_{s-1}],\,W_{2}[y]\big\rangle, | | (1) | where base s \mathrm{base}_{s} denotes the backbone’s logits, and stock DSpark drafts a greedy chain with it. A draft tree contains continuations that the target verifies in one pass, each node seeing only its ancestors, and the step accepts the longest root path matching the target’s argmax plus a bonus token [ 7 ] . DDTree [ 10 ] adds nodes by path log-probability up to N N , so every prefix of this order is a best-first tree ( prefix-closed ). ## 2.3 Hybrid Targets Our main target model, Qwen3.8-27B [ 14 ] , uses Gated DeltaNet (GDN) [ 21 ] in 48 of 64 layers and attention elsewhere. quote: recomputes the recurrent state along each root path instead of storing it per node.
